author: reek
body: A `let` statement in an act block is do-notation: it scopes over the REST of the block, not merely over its own `in` body. This is the other half of the let-scoping fix. The emitter's locals table used to be flat per function, so a sibling statement reading the let's binding resolved by accident -- the binding had simply never been popped. Lowering now nests the remaining statements inside the let's body, which makes the IR say what the language always meant.

author: reek
body: First, a single let statement scopes over the statements after it.

author: reek
body: Second, a let CHAIN (`let a = .. in let b = .. in stmt`) scopes ALL of its bindings over the rest. Peeling only the outermost let leaves the inner ones bound beside the following statements rather than above them, and they fail to resolve -- CDX2040, an unresolved call. That is what `mask-ops` does, and it is how the first attempt at this fix was caught.

author: reek
body: Third, a later let statement of the same name SHADOWS the earlier one for the rest of the block, and only for the rest of the block. A read before it still sees the old binding. This is the do-notation rule and it must hold in the direction that keeps working, not just the one that was broken.

author: reek
body: Fourth, a let bound inside an `if` arm does NOT escape that arm. The arm's binding is popped when the arm ends, so the trailing read finds the outer binding -- the miscompile 2.22 is named for.
